Activation steering works by adding a vector — derived from contrastive pairs or sparse autoencoder features — to a model's residual stream mid-forward-pass, attempting to induce a target behavioral direction. The central question here is: when a model must simultaneously satisfy multiple instructions that pull on overlapping latent directions (e.g., "be maximally helpful" and "refuse harmful content"), does the steering vector reliably compose with those objectives, or does it collapse, amplify one objective at the expense of another, or produce emergent behaviors that neither objective predicts? The key concepts are: the geometry of steering vectors in residual stream space (specifically whether conflicting objectives are linearly separable or entangled), the distinction between shallow behavioral compliance and deep representational change, and the difference between instruction-following as a single learned superposition versus as a dynamic routing problem across layers. A beginner assumes that steering is additive and modular — that you can push "less sycophantic" independently of "more cautious" — but an expert worries about interference in the overcomplete feature basis, where vectors that look orthogonal in activation space actually share downstream computational pathways through attention heads and MLPs, producing side-channel behavioral drift invisible in standard evaluations. The deeper concern is that failure modes aren't random: they're systematically biased toward whichever latent objective has stronger basin attraction in the trained distribution, meaning that steering vectors may appear to work on held-out prompts while silently degrading reliability precisely where compositional pressure is highest.

Behavioral cancellation tells you that the net downstream effect on whatever metric you're measuring (refusal rate, sentiment score, output token distribution) sums to near-zero — but it tells you almost nothing about the geometry directly, because the mapping from residual stream perturbations to behavior is highly nonlinear. Two vectors could cancel behaviorally while being nearly parallel (each pushing the same direction with opposite signs, truly subtracting), or while being nearly orthogonal (each corrupting different computational subgraphs whose behavioral effects happen to offset). Anthropic's dictionary learning work on Claude (Templeton et al., 2024) showed that even single features in the residual stream activate dense downstream circuits — so "cancellation" in behavior space could mask two large, overlapping perturbations that are both doing substantial hidden work on intermediate computations while leaving the final logit distribution roughly intact. A concrete diagnostic failure: if you steer toward "more verbose" and simultaneously toward "more concise," behavioral cancellation on length doesn't mean the vectors subtracted cleanly — probing the residual stream mid-layer may reveal elevated activation norms, suggesting the model is expending representational capacity resolving a conflict rather than passing through unperturbed. What behavioral cancellation specifically cannot tell you is whether the interference is happening at the feature level (superposition collisions), the circuit level (competing attention head routing), or the objective level (the model learned a meta-strategy for trading off the two behaviors that happens to produce neutral output on your eval distribution). Turner et al.'s activation addition work (2023) on GPT-2 found that vector addition effects were surprisingly linear for single vectors on clean prompts, but compositionality was not tested under genuine objective conflict — the linearity result is frequently over-extrapolated to the multi-vector case.

The mechanism isn't norm dilution but representational overwriting: under compositional load, later attention heads are writing large, instruction-relevant vectors into the residual stream that effectively rotate the steered representation away from the target direction, not shrink it. You can distinguish these empirically by measuring the projection of the residual stream onto your steering vector direction at each layer, rather than just the norm: norm dilution would show the residual stream magnitude decreasing while the cosine similarity to the steering vector holds roughly constant, whereas representational overwriting shows cosine similarity collapsing at a specific layer while the overall norm may actually increase due to the new instruction-following content being written in. Hernandez et al.'s fact-editing work (2023) on ROME/MEMIT showed that late MLP layers (roughly layers 15–25 in GPT-2-XL scale models) are critical for binding specific content to behavioral outputs — this is the same region where compositional instruction following likely asserts dominance over an earlier-injected steering vector. A sharper empirical test is to apply the steering vector at progressively later layers and measure the behavioral effect size under both simple and compositional prompts: if the effect gap between conditions narrows when you inject later (closer to output), that localizes the overwriting to earlier-mid layers and rules out the trivial explanation that the vector simply wasn't large enough. What you're really looking for is a "takeover layer" — the earliest layer at which the slope of cosine-similarity decay correlates with instruction complexity — and current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., TransformerLens patch hooks) makes this measurement tractable but it has not been done systematically for steering vector failure under compositional load.

The naive fix breaks because attention heads don't implement behavior — they implement routing decisions whose meaning is context-dependent, so steering a head's output vector directly imposes a fixed routing bias onto a mechanism whose correct operation is precisely to vary its routing based on the current representational context. Concretely: if head L.24.H7 normally routes "instruction-priority" signals under compositional load, steering it toward a fixed output direction doesn't suppress that routing function — it corrupts the key-query geometry that all downstream heads depend on, cascading errors through the remaining layers in ways that are neither predictable nor bounded. Wang et al.'s IOI circuit work (2022) established that even simple two-token indirect object identification involves careful coordination across 26 heads — intervening on one head shifts the effective "vote" but also degrades the signal fidelity that other heads in the circuit rely on, and that degradation scales nonlinearly with how far the intervention vector is from the head's natural output distribution. The breaking point reveals something fundamental: linear interventions assume that the target behavior lives in a stable affine subspace of activation space, but objective integration under compositional instructions is implemented as a dynamic equilibrium across attention layers — the "answer" to competing objectives isn't stored anywhere, it's computed by the interaction pattern itself, and you can't linearly perturb an interaction pattern without dissolving it. This is why Zou et al.'s representation engineering (2023) found that steering works best on properties that correspond to stable, context-invariant directions (e.g., emotional valence, which has consistent geometry across contexts) and degrades on properties requiring contextual arbitration — precisely the regime compositional instruction following lives in. The deeper implication is that the failure mode isn't a bug in the steering methodology but a signal that compositional objective integration may be an irreducibly nonlinear computation, meaning that any linear probe or intervention will have a fundamental accuracy ceiling that no amount of better vector estimation can overcome.

Intervening on the interaction pattern itself means intervening on the attention scores or equivalently on the query-key inner products before softmax — not on any single residual stream vector but on the bilinear form W_Q^T W_K that determines which tokens attend to which. Concretely, this would require constructing a rank-r perturbation to the effective QK matrix conditioned on the current input, which is no longer a fixed vector addition but a data-dependent linear map — closer to what LoRA fine-tuning does (Hu et al., 2022, with typical ranks 4–64) than to activation addition, and critically it requires knowing the current context to compute the right perturbation, defeating the "steer once, apply everywhere" promise of vector-based methods. The principled reason a low-rank approximation may fail is the following: the softmax in attention is a rank-1-updating operation whose output geometry changes discontinuously near saturation boundaries — small perturbations to QK scores near a softmax saturation point produce near-zero output change, while identical perturbations near a softmax decision boundary produce large routing flips, meaning the Jacobian of the attention pattern with respect to any intervention is ill-conditioned and input-dependent in a way that no fixed low-rank matrix can capture uniformly. Anthropic's superposition work implies that the relevant features for objective arbitration are themselves encoded in superposition across many dimensions, so even if you could construct the right bilinear intervention, identifying which QK subspace to perturb requires first solving the feature identification problem that sparse autoencoders are only partially addressing — Templeton et al. (2024) found millions of features in Claude's middle layers, with no clear inventory of which ones govern instruction-priority arbitration specifically. There is a narrow escape hatch: if the nonlinearity is mild enough in the regime of interest, a second-order (quadratic) intervention — perturbing both the residual stream vector and its outer product with a context vector — might capture the leading interaction term, analogous to how kernel methods extend linear classifiers. But this escape hatch closes under genuine compositional conflict precisely because that's the regime where attention softmax is most saturated and most sensitive to perturbation direction, making the quadratic approximation locally accurate but globally unreliable — the same problem that makes adversarial examples persistent under linear defenses.

Evidence that superior routing knowledge is achievable would require demonstrating that an external model can predict, before the forward pass completes, which objective the target model will incorrectly prioritize — and then showing that intervening based on that prediction improves outcomes on held-out compositional conflicts the predictor wasn't trained on. The strongest existing evidence in this direction comes from representation engineering probes: Zou et al. (2023) showed that linear probes trained on honesty/deception contrasts could predict model behavior with >90% accuracy on some tasks, but crucially these probes were trained and evaluated on behaviorally clean distributions where one objective dominates — their generalization to genuine conflict regimes was not tested, which is precisely where the routing knowledge claim needs to hold. There is a structural reason why failure cases are easier: model failures under compositional conflict tend to cluster around a small number of attractor states (sycophantic collapse, refusal generalization, verbosity runaway) that correspond to high-probability basins in the training distribution, making them lower-entropy and therefore more predictable than the full space of "correct" compositional behavior. This asymmetry mirrors the situation in adversarial robustness: it is far easier to find inputs that cause ImageNet classifiers to fail (because failures concentrate near decision boundaries that can be found by gradient) than to certify correctness across the entire input manifold — and the same asymmetry applies here because "correct objective routing" under novel compositional conflict may not exist stably in the training distribution at all, giving the intervener nothing consistent to learn. Concretely, a mechanistic interpretability approach that identified the specific attention heads responsible for sycophancy collapse (analogous to the IOI circuit) could plausibly yield a failure-specific steering fix — but that fix would be a narrow patch on a known failure mode, not evidence of general superior routing knowledge. The uncomfortable implication is that "achievable superior routing knowledge" may be permanently asymmetric: we can learn enough to suppress known failure attractors, but the space of correct compositional behavior is high-dimensional and distribution-dependent in a way that resists the kind of contrastive dataset construction that makes probe-based steering tractable.

The asymmetry is real and structural: interpretability-guided steering is currently a deficit-reduction tool, not a capability-certification tool, for the same reason that it is easier to write a test that catches a specific bug than to prove a program correct — failure modes have compact descriptions while correctness requires specifying behavior over an unbounded input space. The evidence for this is implicit in every major steering paper: Turner et al. (2023), Zou et al. (2023), and Templeton et al. (2024) all demonstrate suppression of identifiable bad behaviors (deception, harmful content, sycophancy) but none demonstrate that the steered model is more reliably correct on novel compositional inputs it wasn't evaluated against — the eval distributions are always anchored to the known failure taxonomy. Closing the asymmetry would require one of three things: first, a proof that correct compositional behavior can be decomposed into a finite set of learnable primitives that compose predictably (essentially a modularity thesis that current evidence does not support); second, a training regime that makes correct behavior itself low-entropy by construction — something like Constitutional AI's iterative self-critique loop (Bai et al., 2022), which attempts to pull correct behavior into a more concentrated distribution, though it does so at the behavioral level rather than the representational level; or third, a formal verification approach that certifies steering interventions over input classes rather than input samples, analogous to abstract interpretation in program analysis, which does not yet exist for transformer activations at scale. The deepest obstacle to closing the asymmetry is that "correct compositional behavior" is not a property of the model alone — it's a property of the model relative to a context-dependent human value function that is itself underspecified, meaning that the target the intervener is trying to hit is not fixed, which makes learning it fundamentally harder than learning the fixed attractor geometry of failure modes. A partial closure might come from scalable oversight methods (Bowman et al., 2022) that use stronger models to label correct behavior on hard compositional cases, effectively compressing the high-dimensional correctness space into a learnable signal — but this defers the problem to the supervisor model's own compositional reliability, which faces the same asymmetry one level up. The honest conclusion is that interpretability-guided steering will likely remain asymmetric until we have a theory of what correct objective integration computes at the mechanistic level, not just what it produces behaviorally — and that theory does not exist yet.
